prompt: A projectile is launched from ground level at an angle to the horizontal. The projectile is tested first in a vacuum and then in air, where air resistance is significant. Launch speed and launch angle are identical in both cases. How do the maximum height and the angle of descent to the ground in air compare to those in a vacuum?
options: Maximum height is smaller in air; angle of descent is steeper in air.
Maximum height is smaller in air; angle of descent is shallower in air.
Maximum height is greater in air; angle of descent is steeper in air.
Maximum height is the same in air; angle of descent is steeper in air.

answer.explanation: Air resistance opposes motion throughout the flight. On the upward journey, downward drag adds to gravity, increasing deceleration and reducing maximum vertical height. On the downward journey, horizontal drag continues to decrease the horizontal velocity, causing the projectile to fall more steeply, so the angle of descent to the horizontal is steeper than in a vacuum.

distractor_explanations: Correct. Drag reduces vertical ascent height and also rapidly reduces horizontal speed, causing a steeper descent angle.
Incorrect. Believes horizontal drag makes the projectile glide flatter rather than drop more steeply.
Incorrect. Suggests drag could somehow increase maximum height, violating conservation of energy.
Incorrect. Fails to recognise that drag acts on the vertical component during the climb, reducing peak height.
hints: Consider the effect of the retarding force on vertical deceleration during the upward phase.
Consider what happens to the horizontal velocity component as the projectile travels through air.
solution: A. Maximum height is smaller in air; angle of descent is steeper in air.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: During the ascent, air resistance has a downward vertical component that reinforces gravity, giving a total downward acceleration greater than g. Hence maximum height is reduced.
Step 2: Air resistance also has a horizontal component that continuously reduces horizontal velocity throughout the flight.
Step 3: Just before landing, horizontal velocity is significantly reduced while vertical velocity is large, so tan(descent angle) = |v_y| / v_x is larger than in a vacuum.
Step 4: This means the angle of descent to the horizontal is steeper in air.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored independently to test qualitative effects of air resistance on trajectory shape.
